title: Watertown NY Seeing Renaissance
author: Holly Korbey
summary: Korbey opens the first profile in her SOL Tracker (the 'science of learning' district tracker she is building) by landing in Watertown, New York, a working-class community of about 30,000 near the Canadian border. The district is moving from a balanced-literacy and inquiry-based model to an explicitly science-of-learning one, and she argues the feature worth noting is that Watertown is not just adopting the science of reading in isolation. Leaders there have tied evidence-based reading practices to cognitive-science-aligned instruction, feedback, and assessment across the system, because they see the science of reading and the science of learning as one continuous body of evidence. Archive note: the email teaser ends here; the rest of the district profile and extended interviews are paywalled. The frame of the second half of the email is Korbey's round-up of the homework open thread from the previous week, which drew more than forty reader comments. The takeaway she pulls forward is that homework is a more complex instructional decision than most critiques of it acknowledge. The conditions under which it is valuable are specific: it has to be doable for the student at the level they are actually working at, tightly connected to what is being taught in class, designed as meaningful practice that moves a skill forward, and structured so that students cannot cognitive-shortcut it through AI. The profile itself begins with Heather Mulford, a third-grade teacher who had spent nearly a decade in Watertown before feeling defeated by the limits of her previous approach. Her diagnosis (quoted verbatim: the kids who got it got it, and the kids who did not just did not, and year after year children who arrived behind left further behind) is the pivot into the district's reform story, which the free portion of the post sets up but does not complete.
points: Rural districts are experiencing instructional innovation at a pace and scale that urban districts struggle to match, because smaller teams can align faster and implement change without bureaucratic friction.
Teacher trust is the bottleneck in any improvement agenda,when teachers see concrete changes in their own teaching and their students' learning, buy-in follows rather than precedes implementation.

Instructional coaching that is embedded in the daily work of teaching (walk-throughs, classroom observations, feedback cycles) produces measurable shifts in practice faster than professional development days.
Districts that reject the 'silver bullet' approach and instead layer multiple coherent initiatives,literacy, math, behavior,create cumulative learning where each domain reinforces the others.
quotes: Watertown, New York, a working-class community of about 30,000 people near the Canadian border, is moving from a largely balanced literacy and inquiry-based learning district to the science of learning. Educators and leaders I spoke with there have a profound respect for their new knowledge, and a palpable, sometimes even emotional desire for change and to make a difference for students.

Why they are on the Tracker: This district is implementing evidence-based practices in reading while also aligning instruction, feedback and assessment with cognitive science on how humans learn. They’re biting off a lot at one time, but leaders see that the science of reading and the science of learning are connected, and want to get every educator moving in the same direction.

One thing I learned from the more than 40 comments (and counting) in the thread is that homework is a complex topic, with different challenges and needs at different ages, and should be given much more thought and attention than many are giving it. Even though I’ll still stand by my original statement that homework can be valuable, especially when seen as meaningful practice.

Educators and parents brought up so many important points: how the homework has to be doable for students, how they have to know exactly what it has to do with what they’re working on in class; it has to be valuable practice that moves skills forward; it has to be AI proof because students are prone to take the cognitive shortcut.
But often kids are getting dragged down by too much homework, or none at all, or homework that doesn’t necessarily support learning goals.

Heather Mulford had been teaching third grade for almost a decade in Watertown, New York, when she began feeling frustrated and defeated. She loved her students in the working-class town near the Canadian border, and was working tirelessly for them. But year after year, they made little academic progress.

The kids who got it, got it, and the kids who didn’t, just didn’t, and I didn’t feel like I was making a difference,” she told me recently. “If they came to me behind, they were going to leave behind—or further behind.” Archived from The Bell Ringer (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
